title: Effects of visual exposure to wood on human affective states, physiological arousal and cognitive performance: A systematic review of randomized trials
review_question: To (1) examine the influence of visual (real or virtual) contact with either real or imitated indoor wooden surfaces on certain stress indicators, that is affective, physiological or cognitive performance outcomes (compared to non-wooden surfaces) and to (2) assess the methodological quality of the reviewed studies.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Published randomized controlled trials in English, assessing at least one physiological, affective, or cognitive performance outcome in response to visual (real or virtual, any duration) wood exposure in indoor environments (real or imitated, with or without tactile/olfactory contact). Control intervention must be visual exposure to non-wood material. Primary outcomes: autonomic nervous system functioning, core affect/emotions/mood, executive functions. Secondary outcomes: central nervous system functioning, non-affective self-report measures (e.g., fatigue, vigilance). No restrictions on publication year, type, design, intervention duration, wood type, or participant characteristics.

findings.antecedent: Visual exposure to wood (real or virtual, indoor wooden surfaces)
findings.consequent: Indicators of human stress (affective, physiological, cognitive performance)
findings.quote: Current evidence suggests that visual wood exposure may improve certain indicators of human stress, but additional research is needed to confirm the existing findings.

findings.antecedent: Longer visual exposure to wood (indoor settings)
findings.quote: Studies with longer exposure times to wood generally observed improved affective states and decreased physiological arousal in wooden settings, but the results are not entirely clear-cut.

findings.antecedent: Shorter visual exposure to wood (indoor settings)
findings.quote: The results of four studies with shorter exposure durations to wood provide relatively little information regarding the influence of wood exposure on indicators of stress.
The results from Fell36 and Burnard and Kutnar46 are promising since both studies found that the physiological arousal of participants is lower in the wooden environments.

Studies from Zhang et al.51,52 and Demattè et al.35 observed more favourable affective states in the wooden environment, but in neither case it is clear if this was influenced by visual or olfactory properties of the experimental room(s).
Only Fell's36 study reported cognitive performance outcome and it did not find any differences between the wooden and non-wooden environments.

findings.antecedent: Not examining multiple dimensions of stress indicators simultaneously
findings.quote: In general, studies are limited by not examining multiple dimensions of stress indicators simultaneously, which limits the interpretability of their findings.

synthesis_conclusions: Current research suggests that visual wood exposure could lead to beneficial outcomes on human affective states, physiological arousal, and cognitive performance, but the evidence is limited.
Studies are limited by not examining multiple dimensions of stress indicators simultaneously, which hinders the interpretability of findings.
Future studies are critical to confirm and expand current findings to support building design recommendations.
evidence_gaps: Need for additional research to confirm existing findings on visual wood exposure and stress indicators.
Lack of studies simultaneously investigating affective, physiological, and cognitive performance outcomes.
Unclear if positive findings are due to visual or olfactory properties of wood.
Need for more robust study designs, including suitable measures of core affect and appropriate tasks assessing executive functions.
Need for studies focusing on stress recovery following induction of stress.
Need for careful control of tactile and olfactory contact with wood in visual exposure studies.
Need for theories to delve deeper into explaining human response to single natural stimuli.
Potential for publication bias due to the small number of included studies.
risk_of_bias_assessment: Assessed using the Cochrane revised risk of bias tool. Overall risk of bias was low in four studies, high in three studies (due to insufficient randomization or selective reporting), and some concerns in two studies (due to missing outcome data).
heterogeneity_sources: Certain studies not controlling for olfactory stimulation.
Variations in exposure duration (short vs. long).
Most studies measured only one or few outcomes.
publication_bias: Publication bias might have had a major effect on the review's findings.
limitations: Only nine studies included, with high overall risk of bias in three, some concerns in two, and low in four.
Specific methodological shortcomings in reviewed studies, including measuring few outcomes.
Unclear attribution of positive findings to visual or olfactory stimulation of wood.
Methodology in restoration studies may suffer from demand characteristics (good-subject effect).
Small number of included studies, potentially influencing conclusions.
Publication bias might have had a major effect on findings.
Limited to studies reported in English.
Search strategy restricted to human response to wood in indoor environments.
Methods of analysis and inclusion criteria were not documented in a registered protocol.

paper_metadata.title: Effects of visual exposure to wood on human affective states, physiological arousal and cognitive performance: A systematic review of randomized trials
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Effects of visual exposure to wood on human affective states, physiological arousal and cognitive performance: A systematic review of randomized trials
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Background Bringing features of nature indoors can positively influence indicators of human stress. Since wood is a natural material, it may produce similar benefits. The objective of the review was to (1) examine the influence of visual (real or virtual) contact with either real or imitated indoor wooden surfaces on certain stress indicators, that is affective, physiological or cognitive performance outcomes (compared to non-wooden surfaces) and to (2) assess the methodological quality of the reviewed studies. Method We conducted a systematic literature search for English articles on Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science, Cochrane Central and Google Scholar on 6 August 2019. The results of the eligible studies were synthesized narratively in light of the identified methodological shortcomings. Results We reviewed nine studies with 386 participants in total. Studies with longer exposure times to wood generally observed improved affective states and decreased physiological arousal in wooden settings, but the results are not entirely clear-cut. We discuss several methodological issues uncovered in the reviewed studies and provide guidelines for future robust research. Conclusions Current evidence suggests that visual wood exposure may improve certain indicators of human stress, but additional research is needed to confirm the existing findings.
